title: Try/Catch/Finally
description: Master C#'s core exception-handling constructs — try, catch, finally, and using — and understand the precise execution flow when exceptions occur.

data.text: C# provides structured exception handling through the `try`, `catch`, and `finally` blocks. Together, they let you write code that handles errors gracefully, performs mandatory cleanup, and keeps your application running when things go wrong.

A **try** block wraps code that might throw an exception. One or more **catch** blocks follow it, each handling a specific type of error. An optional **finally** block runs regardless of whether an exception occurred — it is the place for cleanup code that must always execute, such as closing a file or releasing a database connection.

data.caption: Execution flow through try, catch, and finally blocks
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    Start([Start]) --> Try[Try block executes]
    Try --> Success{Did exception occur?}
    Success -->|No| Finally[Finally block runs]
    Success -->|Yes| Catch{Catch block matches?}
    Catch -->|Yes| Handle[Caught block runs]
    Catch -->|No| Propagate[Exception propagates up stack]
    Handle --> Finally
    Finally --> End([End])
    Propagate --> End

data.text: The simplest form wraps risky code in a `try` block and catches any exception with a general `catch (Exception)` block. This prevents crashes, but it is imprecise — you won't know which specific error occurred unless you inspect the exception's `Message` property.

data.title: Basic Try/Catch Structure
data.content: The fundamental pattern: wrap risky code in try, handle errors in catch.

data.text: Multiple `catch` blocks can follow a single `try`. The runtime evaluates them top to bottom, executing the first one whose exception type matches. Because `Exception` is the base of all exceptions, it must come last — otherwise it would catch every exception before the more specific handlers get a chance.

data.title: Multiple Catch Blocks
data.content: Handling different exceptions with specific catch blocks and a general fallback.

data.title: Order Matters
data.text: Always place the most specific catch blocks first and the most general (`Exception`) last. C# requires more specific types to appear before their base types. Reversing the order causes a compile error.

Each `catch` block can optionally name a variable that holds the thrown exception. You can use this variable to read the `Message`, `StackTrace`, or any custom properties the exception provides. Naming it (e.g., `ex` or `exception`) is a convention that improves readability.

data.title: Using the Exception Variable
data.content: Reading exception properties to provide useful feedback and log diagnostic details.

data.text: The `finally` block runs whether or not an exception occurred. It is the right place for cleanup code that must execute no matter what — closing database connections, releasing file handles, resetting application state, or disposing resources.

data.title: Finally Block Guarantees
items: Runs after the try block if no exception was thrown
Runs after the catch block if an exception was caught
Runs even if the try or catch contains a return statement
Runs even if you call Environment.Exit (in most cases)

data.title: Finally for Resource Cleanup
data.content: Using finally to ensure a StreamReader is always closed, even if reading fails.

data.title: Prefer the using Statement
data.text: While finally works, C# provides a cleaner alternative. The `using` statement (or `using var` declaration) automatically calls `Dispose()` at the end of the scope. It is equivalent to try/finally with manual disposal, but more readable and less error-prone.

data.title: Using Statement — Automatic Disposal
data.content: The using statement automatically disposes resources, making try/finally unnecessary for disposable objects.

data.text: C# 6 introduced **exception filters** — a condition added after the `catch` type using the `when` keyword. The catch block only executes if the condition is true. When the condition is false, the runtime continues checking the next catch block. Unlike putting logic inside the catch body, filters don't consume the exception — the stack trace remains intact.

data.title: Exception Filters with 'when'
data.content: Using exception filters to catch exceptions conditionally without modifying the stack trace.

data.text: Sometimes you catch an exception to log it or perform partial cleanup, but you still want it to propagate up the stack. You have two options: `throw;` (preserves the original stack trace) and `throw ex;` (resets the stack trace to the current location). Always use `throw;` to preserve debugging information.

cards.title: throw;
cards.description: Rethrows the original exception, preserving its stack trace
pros: You can find where the error originally occurred
cons: Cannot add new information to the exception

cards.title: throw ex;
cards.description: Rethrows the exception but resets the stack trace to this location
pros: Can assign a new exception object
cons: Harder to debug — origin point becomes the rethrow line

data.title: Rethrowing with Stack Trace Preservation
data.content: Logging an exception and rethrowing it correctly to preserve the original stack trace.

data.title: Anti-patterns to Avoid
items: Catching Exception just to swallow it silently — always log or rethrow
Using exceptions for normal control flow (e.g., checking if a user exists)
Catching and doing nothing — this hides bugs
Putting the entire method body inside a try block — be specific about what might fail
Rethrowing with `throw ex;` — always use `throw;` instead

terms.definition: A block of code that is monitored for exceptions. If an exception occurs inside it, control is passed to a matching catch block.
A block that handles exceptions of a specific type. Multiple catch blocks can follow one try block.
A block that always executes after try (and catch), regardless of whether an exception occurred. Used for mandatory cleanup.
A C# construct that ensures a disposable object's Dispose() method is called when the scope ends. Syntactic sugar for try/finally.
A `when` condition on a catch block that must evaluate to true for that block to execute. Does not consume the exception.
Re-emitting a caught exception so it propagates further up the call stack. Use `throw;` to preserve the stack trace.

data.title: Practice: Build a Robust File Reader
data.description: Write a method that reads a text file and returns its contents. Handle FileNotFoundException, DirectoryNotFoundException, UnauthorizedAccessException, and general IOException with appropriate user messages. Use a using statement for the file handle.
steps: Create a method ReadFile(string path) that returns string
Wrap the file reading logic in a try block
Add specific catch blocks for each exception type listed above
Use a using statement for the StreamReader
In each catch block, print a clear message to the user explaining what went wrong
Test with a valid file, a missing file, and an unreadable file
data.expectedOutcome: You will write production-quality error-handling code with specific catch blocks and proper resource cleanup, and understand when each exception type is triggered.

items.text: I understand what each block (try, catch, finally) does
items.hint: try = risky code, catch = error handling, finally = cleanup

items.text: I can write multiple catch blocks for different exception types
I know what the finally block guarantees
items.hint: It runs whether or not an exception occurs, even after return

items.text: I can use the using statement instead of manual try/finally
I know the difference between throw; and throw ex;
items.hint: throw; preserves stack trace; throw ex; does not

items.text: I can use exception filters with the when keyword

items.hint: Always log or rethrow — never catch and do nothing

items.question: Can I use try/catch without catch?
items.answer: No, not directly. If you only want a finally block, you can use try/finally without catch. For try/catch you must have at least one catch block.

items.question: What happens if I have a return inside the try block?
items.answer: The finally block still runs. The return value is held, finally executes, and then the method returns. This is why finally is the right place for cleanup — it runs even if you return early.

items.question: Should I catch all exceptions with one generic catch block?
items.answer: No. Catch specific exception types that you can actually handle. Use a generic `catch (Exception ex)` only as a last-resort safety net near the top of your stack.

items.question: Does using replace try/catch entirely?
items.answer: No. using only replaces try/finally for disposing resources. You still need try/catch to handle errors. using is about cleanup, not error handling.

items.question: What is the performance cost of try/catch?
items.answer: There is essentially no performance cost when no exception occurs. The cost comes when an exception is thrown and the stack is unwound, which is already an expensive operation by nature.

data.title: Lesson Summary
points: The try block wraps code that might throw; catch handles the exception; finally always runs for cleanup
Multiple catch blocks can handle different exception types — place the most specific first
The exception object (commonly named 'ex') gives you Message, StackTrace, and more
Finally is guaranteed to run — even after a return statement or an unhandled exception
The using statement is syntactic sugar for try/finally and should be preferred for disposable resources
Exception filters (when keyword) let catch blocks fire conditionally without consuming the exception
Use throw; to rethrow — it preserves the original stack trace for debugging
data.takeaway: Mastering try/catch/finally is essential for building C# applications that are resilient, debuggable, and safe to run in production.
